newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Mood muted in Taiwan town hosting Dalai Lama visit.
newsitem.headline: Mood muted in Taiwan town hosting Dalai Lama visit.

text.p: On the eve of the Dalai Lama's arrival in Taiwan, the political bluster surrounding the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader's visit appeared to have caused discomfort in the town of Kaohsiung, his first stop.

Far from making a great fuss about the Tibetan Buddhist god-king's arrival on Saturday, Kaohsiung on Friday seemed as if it were taking pains to play down the visit that has infuriated communist China.
"I just don't see why it's such a serious issue," said Chang Pao-wen, a housewife and Kaohsiung resident, echoing comments of many citizens interviewed in the southern port city's bustling streets.
"They (China) are making much too much of it. He's just a religious leader who's making a religious visit," she said.

China attacked the Dalai Lama's visit and his expected March 27 meeting with President Lee Teng-hui as collusion by two "splittists" whose aim is independence for both Tibet and Taiwan from the communist mainland.

Beijing maintains that Taiwan, split from the mainland by civil war in 1949, and Tibet, where the crushing of an anti-Chinese uprising in 1959 forced the Dalai Lama into exile in India, have been part of China for centuries.

At harbourside Sun Yat-sen University, where the Dalai Lama receives an honorary doctorate on Sunday, the only signs of his imminent arrival were two modest posters hung among scores of others advertising everything from classical music to gay coffee gatherings.
"I don't think a lot of students know much about the visit," said a young woman helping to organise the ceremony.

Unlike the capital Taipei where businesses have erected huge displays to welcome the Dalai Lama when he travels there on Sunday night, Kaohsiung was eerily empty of Dalai Lama fanfare with the exception of scores of new national flags flying at the city stadium where speaks on Saturday.

An organiser from the sponsoring Chinese Buddhist Association said she was not surprised that students and civic groups had not organised welcoming activities despite Taiwan's reputation for warm hospitality.
"Aside from us practising Buddhists, I doubt that ordinary people would know about the Dalai Lama's visit," she said.

Others disagreed, saying Kaohsiung residents were fully aware that organisers had chosen their city for the Dalai Lama's first Taiwan stop but were deeply uncomfortable about the political fracas surrounding his stay.

An environmental researcher said Taiwan's pro-independence opposition was hoping to capitalise on the visit to promote their cause by putting Tibet's quest for independence from China on the same level as Taiwan's.

"This is a very sensitive issue and everyone knows it," the researcher said. "But independence for Taiwan is one thing. Independence for Tibet is another. They have nothing to do with one another, so why mix them together?"
Taxi driver Tsai Chieh-chao said local people were worried that Taiwan's feuding political parties would blow the visit out of proportion.
"Everyone knows the Dalai Lama is coming, but people are hoping it won't escalate," Tsai said.
Chang Tien-chen, who runs a shop selling Buddhist wares, said she felt sorry for the 1989 Nobel peace laureate and wished that his visit could take place without political overtones.
"Taiwan is very lucky to have a visit by such a splendid religious leader," she said. "To see this occasion turned into something else, something political, I think that's really unfortunate."
